source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 4 and ch. 8 (ACH)
finding: Heuer defines diagnosticity as how much an item of evidence helps decide between hypotheses. Evidence consistent with all hypotheses has little or no diagnostic value. Most of the evidence for a favoured hypothesis is often also consistent with the rivals. ACH step 3 works across the matrix one evidence item at a time; step 4 deletes non-diagnostic rows; step 6 re-checks the few linchpin items that drive the result.
numbers: Optional numeric refinement: ask 'if this hypothesis is true, what is the probability I would see this item?' per cell. Worked example is hypothetical (Iraq retaliation: E1 = Saddam statement, consistent with all, no value; E4 = radio broadcasts, diagnostic).
quote: A high temperature may have great value in telling a doctor that a patient is sick, but relatively little value in determining which illness
limits: The text calls ACH 'a surprisingly effective, proven process' with no experiment cited. The matrix uses ordinal marks, not likelihood ratios. Heuer says people cannot hold 3 to 7 hypotheses in working memory, which is the motive for the tool.
agent_relevance: Defines the S7 discriminating test in plain terms: rank candidate tests by how differently the live hypotheses predict them, drop tests all hypotheses predict alike. Code can hold the matrix; the model cannot be trusted to.

source: Heuer (1999) ch. 8 step 5: reject rather than confirm
finding: ACH sums inconsistency, not support. Work down each hypothesis column looking for evidence that rejects it. The hypothesis with the least inconsistent evidence is favoured. Heuer says this forces more time on the seemingly less likely hypotheses.
numbers: No numbers. Step 6 sensitivity: ask what the conclusion becomes if each linchpin item were wrong or deceptive.
limits: Mandel et al. 2018 later argue that ignoring support in aggregation is a misapplication of Popper and hurts probability judgment (see b03 and b05).
agent_relevance: Rejection-only scoring is a design choice to test, not to copy. Keep both support and inconsistency, and score by likelihood ratio in code.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
finding: Randomised test of ACH on 50 UK intelligence analysts. ACH did not improve accuracy and was a little worse than no technique. But the ACH group rated how useful each cue was far better than the control group.
numbers: N = 50 (25 per arm). Task: 4 tribes A-D, base rates 5/20/30/45%, 12 probabilistic cues. MAE ACH 0.26 vs control 0.21, d = 0.43, p = .14 (medium effect, not significant). Usefulness ratings vs true probability gain: r = .68 (ACH) vs .17 (control), d = 1.59, p < .001.
limits: Analysts averaged 14 months experience; hypothetical task with exact numeric cues; control group not told to use any method; ACH group had just been trained, control had not.
agent_relevance: People can learn to rank evidence by diagnostic value when forced to externalise it. Ranking skill did not carry into better final probabilities, so the agent should use the ranking to pick the test and compute the posterior in code.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) accuracy link to diagnosticity ratings
finding: Among ACH users, how well they tracked cue usefulness had no link to their final accuracy. Among control analysts the link existed and was medium to large.
numbers: Correlation of usefulness-tracking with MAE: ACH r(24) = -.10, p = .63; control r(24) = -.42, p = .045; pooled r(49) = -.14.
limits: Small cells (24 df). Authors suspect the consistency-encoding phase puts the analyst in an evidence-contingent frame rather than a hypothesis-contingent one.
agent_relevance: Knowing which evidence is diagnostic is not enough. A scaffold that only asks the model to label diagnosticity may not raise accuracy; the label must be used by code to change what is tested or how it is scored.

source: Mandel et al. (2018) coherence and unpacking
finding: Analysts' four tribe probabilities summed far above 1 in both arms, worse with ACH. Implicit disjunctions got less probability than the sum of their parts.
numbers: Mean sum of the four MECE probabilities: control 1.54 (d = 0.96), ACH 1.77 (d = 1.69), both p < .001. Accuracy difference favoured control with probability of superiority .62 (d = 0.45).
limits: Support-theory unpacking effect. ACH does not check additivity, so it cannot catch this.
agent_relevance: G5 in the schema (code normalises probabilities) is supported. Never let the model emit hypothesis probabilities that are not renormalised.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) post-analytic fixes
finding: What worked was statistical, not procedural. Forcing judgments to be coherent, then averaging across analysts, cut error by 61%.
numbers: Raw MAE 0.23 to 0.15 after coherentizing (35% cut, d = 0.96). Coherentize then equal-weight average of all 50 analysts: MAE 0.09 (61% cut). Plain normalising (divide by the sum) gave MAE 0.13. Most aggregation gain came from about 3 analysts.
limits: One task, one vector of truth values. Aggregation partly removes variance, not only bias (see b09).
agent_relevance: Supports code-side normalisation and several independent attempts, with the G4 caveat that samples from one model are not independent analysts.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
finding: ACH gave no coherence advantage over a no-technique control when evidence was uncertain (source reliability and information credibility varied). ACH users also showed pseudo-diagnostic weighting: evidence rated non-diagnostic still moved their consistency scores.
numbers: N = 227 Canadian graduates, 6 cases, 2 hypotheses. Non-diagnostic evidence had about 32% of the impact of fully diagnostic evidence (intercept .233, total .735, slope B = .502, R2 = .055). Recoded so consistent = positive: about 30%. ACH less reliable across isomorphic cases: MAD .22 vs .18, d = 0.20, p = .051.
limits: Control group did not give consistency ratings, so the same bias may exist there. Online panel, not analysts. Evidence described in words, not numbers.
agent_relevance: Direct number for the failure mode S7 must avoid: about one third of weight leaks to evidence that cannot separate hypotheses. A code check that sets the weight of a non-discriminating item to zero removes it.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) wording and conservatism
finding: Both arms were subadditive for binary complements as total evidential support rose, and too conservative compared with a Bayesian posterior built from each person's own reading of the uncertainty words.
numbers: Elicited normalised probabilities agreed with the Bayesian posterior on the favoured hypothesis in every case (case 3 a tie) but were less extreme. Match rate overall .74 [.70, .77]; ACH vs control difference d = 0.15, p = .25.
limits: Word-to-number meaning was elicited per person.
agent_relevance: Expect under-extreme answers when the agent weighs evidence. Do not extremise votes (G4), but let code compute the update from stated likelihoods.

source: Karvetski, Mandel and Irwin (2020) Improving probability judgment in intelligence analysis: from structured analysis to statistical aggregation
finding: ACH and a factorised-Bayes method (FBT) both failed to handle correlated evidence. ACH users double counted a cue that was perfectly correlated with an earlier one, and more so when the redundancy was made salient. ACH also lowered coherence and accuracy compared with the same people before the method.
numbers: N = 147, mushroom-species task, two perfectly correlated cues. Double counting in ACH: 25% (low salience, n = 20) vs 57% (high salience, n = 21), p = .037. FBT condition: conditional-probability distance 0.27 (low) vs 0.14 (high), d = 0.56, p = .036. Coherentization gave about 1 SD error cut; most aggregation gain by group size 10.
limits: Preprint version (8 pages, OSF). No training given on either method. Crowd members were not experts.
agent_relevance: Diagnosticity is not additive when evidence is correlated. S7 must group dependent tests (same attempt, same model, same source) and count a group once. This is the code-side form of G4.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) Critical review of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses technique
finding: Review found seven articles describing six experiments of ACH and concluded ACH as a whole has little to no benefit and may harm. Some parts (listing all cues, building a matrix, rating diagnosticity) may help.
numbers: Study sizes: Lehner 2008 N = 24; Mandel 2018 N = 50; Karvetski 2020 N = 147; Whitesmith 2018 N = 39 (32 students, 7 UK intelligence staff); Maegherman 2021 N = 191, of whom only 38% of ACH participants reported using the matrix. Lehner: ACH cut confirmation bias for people with no analytic experience but not for experienced analysts.
limits: Small and heterogeneous studies. Authors flag low power, and the ACH arms differ between studies. Not a meta-analysis, no pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: No evidence that the whole procedure helps. Evidence for parts: externalising evidence and diagnosticity ratings. Our S7 should be the minimal part (the discriminating item), not the 8-step ritual.

source: Dhami, Belton and Mandel (2019) The analysis of competing hypotheses in intelligence analysis (as summarised in Wilcox and Mandel 2023)
finding: Same 50-analyst dataset, looked at strategy use. Most ACH analysts deviated from at least one ACH step, especially by adding up consistent evidence. Most control analysts built an ACH-style matrix unprompted (16 of 25). ACH users used base rates less.
numbers: 16/25 control analysts spontaneously built a matrix. ACH group listed all cues correctly more often but used base rates less than control.
limits: Second-hand summary from the review; the original paper was not opened (publisher blocked).
agent_relevance: A diagnostic matrix is a natural human strategy. The harmful part was the rule to ignore base rates and support. Keep the prior in the update.

source: Whitesmith (2018) The efficacy of ACH in mitigating serial position effects and confirmation bias (as summarised in Wilcox and Mandel 2023)
finding: ACH did not significantly reduce serial-position or confirmation bias in an intelligence-style scenario. Confirmation bias also changed how people used ACH's scoring.
numbers: Participants about 39 (32 university, 7 UK intelligence community). Confirmation bias scored by five criteria, for example diagnosticity ratings bending toward prior belief and low-credibility items raising belief.
limits: Summary from the review only. Small sample. It is unclear how many of the five criteria defined bias.
agent_relevance: Diagnosticity ratings are themselves contaminated by prior belief. In the agent, rate diagnosticity before seeing which hypothesis is leading, or let code compute it from separately elicited likelihoods.

source: D'Addario and Macchi (2012) Pseudodiagnosticity: the role of the rarity factor
finding: Large conceptual replication of the car-problem pseudodiagnosticity task. Only 30% to 31% chose the normatively correct cell B. The rarity effect reported by Feeney, Evans and Venn was not found. What mattered was whether the two features differed in how informative they looked, and whether the given percentage was low.
numbers: N = 240, 6 versions, 40 per version, between subjects. Cell B choice: rare first feature 30% vs common first feature 31.3% (chi2 = .039, ns). Features differing in rarity: 40% vs 25.6% (chi2(1) = 5.207, p < .05). Given percentage low 40.8% vs high 20% (chi2(1) = 12.304, p < .001).
limits: Italian students, one task family; a pretest picked features seen as informative. Disputes rarity-as-heuristic and supports a perceived-informativeness account.
agent_relevance: Whether a model asks for the missing likelihood (cell B) may depend on the surface numbers shown, not on the logic. Present the 2x2 likelihood table as code output so every cell is visible.

source: Feeney, Evans and Venn (2000a, 2008) rarity and pseudodiagnosticity (as reported in D'Addario and Macchi 2012)
finding: When the first datum was a rare feature, many more people asked for the same feature under the rival hypothesis, so the usual pseudodiagnostic error shrank.
numbers: Car problem, rare feature (top speed over 165 mph) vs common feature (radio): 43% chose cell B (correct), 44% chose cell C (pseudodiagnostic). Same result with 10% instead of 80% given for cell A.
limits: Second-hand figures taken from the replication paper; originals not opened. D'Addario and Macchi (b13) only partly replicate. Rarity may act through perceived informativeness.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition. Rare, surprising evidence prompts the alternative-hypothesis check. Common evidence does not, so the agent needs an explicit trigger for common evidence.

source: Doherty, Mynatt, Tweney and Schiavo (1979) Pseudodiagnosticity (as described in D'Addario and Macchi 2012)
finding: Founding study. Given P(datum | favoured hypothesis), people asked next for another datum about the same hypothesis (cell C) rather than the same datum under the rival (cell B), which is the one needed for the likelihood ratio.
numbers: No numbers recorded: original paper not opened (paywalled).
limits: Only the secondary description was read. Later accounts tie the error to a working-memory limit of one hypothesis at a time (Mynatt, Doherty and Dragan 1993) and to a dual-process failure of explicit reasoning (Evans, Venn and Feeney 2002).
agent_relevance: The agent analogue is asking again whether the favoured hypothesis predicts X, instead of what the rival predicts for X. S7 should force the rival's likelihood as the next query.

source: Nelson (2005) Finding useful questions: on Bayesian diagnosticity, probability, impact and information gain
finding: Metadata only, paper not opened. It compares measures of how useful a question is: Bayesian diagnosticity, probability gain, impact, information gain. A later paper (Nelson, McKenzie, Cottrell and Sejnowski 2010, Experience Matters) follows up on probability gain.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not read; do not cite results from it until opened. Crossref listed 164 citations at the time of search.
agent_relevance: The choice of score matters. A likelihood-ratio score can rank a test highly that rarely changes the answer. Pick the score on purpose and test it on our own data.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori and Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating inductive reasoning in LLMs with rule discovery games
finding: Twelve LLMs played 100 semantic rule-discovery games where the first hypothesis is narrower than the truth, so only a test outside the hypothesis (negative test) can reject it. Reasoning models did much better. The share of positive tests (confirmation bias) predicted failure.
numbers: Success: best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33% to 35%; GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%; small reasoning models worse (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%). Success vs confirmation bias Spearman rho = -0.779, p = .003. Positive-test share 24% to 39% for reasoning models vs 66% to 82% for instruction-tuned. Bayesian mixed logistic model (n = 1,200 games): confirmation bias coefficient -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error -0.12 (no effect).
limits: Each LLM also served as oracle, human check on 1 triple and 1 guess per game, oracle accuracy 85% to 95%. Only the case where the hypothesis is a subset of the truth is tested; Klayman and Ha (1987) say positive tests can falsify when the hypothesis is broader than the truth.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent measurement that a discriminating test (one where hypotheses disagree) drives success. Supports S7. Condition: use negative-test pressure when the working rule may be too narrow.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench turn-level failure
finding: Even models that tested well often failed to move off a wrong hypothesis. Failure was tied to how models walk the hypothesis space, not only to the share of positive tests.
numbers: Conclusive falsification rate per test turn: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%. Correlation with confirmation bias rho = -0.937, p < .001. Within-model: GPT-5.2-Chat bias 20% in won games vs 50% in lost; GPT-OSS-20B 17% vs 53%.
limits: Hypothesis-to-target relation labelled by GPT-5-Mini, not a human, for all turns.
agent_relevance: A test counts only if its result could force a revision. Log, per test, whether any live hypothesis could have been rejected by it (a code check), and drop tests that cannot reject anything.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky and Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Eleven LLMs on a Wason 2-4-6 style rule discovery task showed confirmation bias. Less bias went with more success. Prompting with human debiasing instructions raised discovery from 42% to 56% on average.
numbers: Success 6% to 78% (45-turn limit). Think-in-Opposites raised success in all 11 model-mode settings; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. Examples: Qwen3-32B non-thinking baseline 0.33, Dual-Goal 0.10; Qwen3-8B thinking baseline 0.21 with incompatible-to-compatible test ratio 0.15. Changes significant for thinking models, mixed for non-thinking. 80 episodes per model-variant.
limits: Dual-Goal can hurt non-thinking models, so the instruction is not safe everywhere. Numeric triples only; a second task (Blicket) is in the same paper.
agent_relevance: Counterexample prompting works for some models and harms others. Test per model before adding it to S7 (G7: must pay for itself). Do not add it for non-reasoning backbones without a check.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) distilling the debiasing behaviour
finding: Fine-tuning a model on traces produced under the Think-in-Opposites prompt raised success without the prompt, and carried over partly to a new task.
numbers: Qwen3-8B baseline 0.21; within-size intervention distillation 0.35; Qwen3-32B baseline 0.41, distilled 0.64; teacher prompt alone 0.36 (8B) and 0.61 (32B); cross-scale (32B teacher to 8B) with intervention 0.59, almost triple the 8B baseline. Blicket test set 192 episodes.
limits: Requires training. Our agent is scaffold only, so this is context.
agent_relevance: Shows the behaviour is learnable and not only a prompt effect, but the scaffold route should suffice if the check is done in code.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath and Hwu (2024) WILT: a multi-turn memorisation-robust inductive logic benchmark
finding: Models must find a hidden boolean rule over three numbers by proposing tests. Even the best model solved only 28%. Models differ in whether they narrow the hypothesis space or infer the rule from results, and many repeat tests that cover already-matched cases.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50, o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Llama 3.1 405B 8/50, GPT-4o-mini 6/50 with 27.22 guesses and 9.78 repeats on average.
limits: Late-2024 models, 50 puzzles per model, numeric rules only; reasoning models did not dominate.
agent_relevance: Repeats show models fail to track which hypotheses a test already separated. Keep a code ledger of tested inputs and the partition each induced (G12 history).

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Choosing each question by expected information gain, with the LLM giving likelihoods and code doing the arithmetic, beat letting the LLM pick questions by prompt in a 20 Questions game.
numbers: Three sets of 100 targets (Animals, Celebrities, Things), six LLMs. Mean success gain 37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; more than doubled in over half the setups, never decreased. Success %: Animals GPT-4o 45 to 93; Celebrities Mistral-Large 19 to 91; Things GPT-4o 34 to 64; Things Llama-3.1-8B 10 to 26. Split baseline on Animals GPT-4o 83.
limits: Answerer is also an LLM, not a human. Preference-elicitation task showed smaller gains and Prompt-Only was a stronger baseline there. Needs a hypothesis set that can be filtered for consistency.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for the S7 design: sample hypotheses, have the model give P(outcome | hypothesis), compute information gain in code, then ask. Filter hypotheses that contradict the history.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM ablations
finding: Each part mattered: expected information gain beat marginal predictive entropy, and keeping only hypotheses consistent with the history beat generating them without filtering.
numbers: Same tables: Entropy ablation below full BED-LLM in most cells (Animals Llama-3.3-70B 68 vs 79; Celebrities Qwen2.5-72B 59 vs 84; Celebrities GPT-4o 64 vs 86). In-context Beliefs ablation Animals GPT-4o 25 vs 93.
limits: Intervals about +/- 3 to 5 points at 100 targets per cell.
agent_relevance: A test whose outcome is uncertain is not the same as a test that separates hypotheses. Use the expected-information-gain form, not the entropy of the answer.

source: Grand, Pepe, Tenenbaum and Andreas (2026) Shoot first, ask questions later? Building rational agents that explore and act like people (ICLR 2026)
finding: In Collaborative Battleship, most LMs ask poor questions: many have zero information gain. Selecting questions by sampled expected information gain let small models beat humans and a frontier model at about 1% of its cost.
numbers: Humans N = 42 (accuracy 92.5%; mean EIG 0.351 bits, median 0.411; ceiling 0.531). Zero-EIG questions: Llama-4-Scout 18.5%, GPT-4o 14.6%. Spotter accuracy up to +14.7 points (GPT-4.1 75.2 to 90.9; Claude 4 Opus 86.8 to 94.4). Captain EIG up to +0.227 bits (94.2% of noise ceiling). Targeting F1 Llama-4-Scout 0.367 to 0.764, GPT-4o 0.450 to 0.782. Win rate Llama-4-Scout 8% to 82% vs humans, 0% to 67% vs GPT-5. Guess Who? replication +28.3 to +42.4 points.
limits: Game with an exactly sampleable board space. GPT-5 itself did not gain much. Gains need a code-side world model for the likelihoods.
agent_relevance: Second independent confirmation. Roughly 1 in 6 questions from some models cannot change belief at all. Score each candidate S7 test by sampled information gain and drop zero-gain tests before running them.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu and van der Schaar (2025) Active task disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Framing clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design (pick the question with the most information gain over candidate solutions) gave better disambiguation than reasoning only in question space.
numbers: Code generation (HumanEval, APPS), 4 elicited requirements; GPT-4o-mini zero-shot on APPS only 35% vs 70% on HumanEval. EIG-based strategies gave higher accuracy with fewer questions; the gap to baseline prompts is smaller for more capable models.
limits: Exact figures sit in figures and appendix tables not reproduced here. The BED-LLM paper says its own baseline did much better than the one reported here.
agent_relevance: Benefit of explicit hypothesis-space reasoning shrinks as the base model improves, so G7 applies: measure at equal tokens against the current backbone.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen and van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly. In a five-round flight-recommendation task most showed little improvement after the first round. Chain-of-thought and other prompting did not close the gap. Training the model to copy a Bayesian assistant did.
numbers: 624 simulated users, 5 rounds, 100 test sets per round; human subset 48 users. Fine-tuned models agreed with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time, more than original or oracle-tuned models.
limits: Fine-tuning study on Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5 (7B to 70B), not frontier closed models.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model to hold and update a posterior. Let code carry the posterior; the model supplies single likelihood judgments.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: On the Wason selection task, a classic test of seeking the card that can falsify the rule, LLMs and humans were both poor and both did better with realistic content than with arbitrary rules.
numbers: Realistic-content advantage significant in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5 (all z > 2.2, p < .03); marginal in PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 (z up to 1.78, p up to .08). Most human subjects were at or below chance; slower humans were above chance only on realistic rules.
limits: 2022 to 2024 models; a selection task on a stated rule, not an open search. Not a test of the newest reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Content familiarity, not logic, drives which test gets picked. Abstract, unfamiliar hypothesis sets (like ARC items) are the hard case for S7.
